title: No. 10 Penn State women’s volleyball sweeps UConn in Rec Hall opener
author: Elliott Inscho | Sports Editor
description:
Volleyball season is officially back in Happy Valley, and Penn State opened its 2026 campaign with a bang.

The Nittany Lions cruised to a three-set sweep over UConn on Saturday, opening the regular season on the right foot after falling to SMU in an exhibition during the Spikes Under the Lights tournament.

“It was a great crowd tonight,” Katie Schumacher-Cawley said. “It's always nice to win. It's hard to win, and I thought we did a nice job. Collectively as a team, we did some nice things.”

Alexis Stucky electrified a roaring Rec Hall crowd early in her home debut, winning consecutive points on a block and ace to open the first set. After UConn won a pair of points, she made her first assist on a pass to Ryla Jones, who made a smooth swing to put Penn State up 4-2.

Coming off a 12-kill outing against SMU on Thursday, Whitney Lauenstein got her first of the match on another assist from Stucky before Kennedy Martin got on the board to follow.

After beginning her career with Nebraska and Texas, Lauenstein was impressed by Saturday’s raucous crowd during her first time playing in front of them.

“I think they bring a lot of energy and it's a lot of fun,” Lauenstein said. “I'd love to see them at 10 a.m. tomorrow. It's definitely fun to be on the same side as them. I’ve played against them, but it feels good to be with them rooting for you this time.”

UConn won back-to-back points, but the blue and white responded with three of their own, forcing head coach Ellen Herman-Kimball to call her first timeout with the Huskies down 10-5.

It didn’t do much. Penn State rattled off three more points on an ace from Haley Burgdorf and kills from Stucky and Lauenstein to cap a 6-0 run. UConn finally ended the stretch when Maja Daca made a kill to cut the Nittany Lion lead to seven.

Schumacher-Cawley made the choice to start Burgdorf in her first home game, and it paid off. She made six kills on a .346% clip and posted six digs, all while only finding out she’d be in the starting lineup during warmups.

“I think sometimes I'll come out nervous, but I do try to hide it kind of well,” Burgdorf said. “But after a couple points, I'm ready to get after it and win the game. Just being calm and collected is my strong suit, and relying on my teammates that they’ve got my back.”

The blue and white won two of the next three points heading into the media timeout, highlighted by Lauenstein’s third kill of the set off Stucky’s ninth assist.

Back-to-back action brought the Penn State lead to 17-9, before the Nittany Lions went on a 3-0 run that ended with a Lexi Gin service error. Stucky continued her strong Rec Hall opener with a quick flick over the net that gave Penn State a 22-12 advantage late in the set.

UConn didn’t go down easy in the first set, though. Freshman middle blocker Courtney Grayson rejected a powerful swing from Lauenstein and made a kill of her own to keep things interesting down the stretch, but a block from Martin and Jones clinched the set for Penn State.

Stucky’s set-opening serve went long, setting the tone for a stretch where the Huskies won three of four points. Penn State responded with a dominant five-point run to regain the lead.

After a challenge reversed what looked to be a Penn State point, Gabrielle Nichols answered with an emphatic spike to give her squad a 9-6 lead. This started a four-point run that also saw two attack errors and a kill from Stucky, resulting in another timeout from Herman-Kimball.

The longtime leader’s second respite shifted momentum, as the Huskies won eight of ten points to follow. UConn’s run brought the set level at 14-14 and led to Schumacher-Cawley’s first timeout.

Things stayed tight, but Penn State started to pull away on a four-point run highlighted by a dig from Martin that led to a Nichols kill. It wasn’t quite over yet, though.

Another late-set kill from Grayson and back-to-back aces cut Penn State’s lead to 22-21. However, Lauenstein and Martin fired off consecutive kills before a combined block by the Nittany Lions won them the second set.

UConn opened the third frame similarly to the set preceding it, taking a 3-2 lead early before a five-point run by Penn State saw the Nittany Lions jump out to a commanding 7-3 lead. UConn finally ended the scoring drought on a service error from libero Ava Faltudo.

Freshman middle blocker Kendall Northern notched her second kill of the match, before the Huskies won four of five points, tightening Penn State’s advantage to 9-8. UConn began a four-point run after that, taking a two-point lead before Lauenstein recorded a kill to end the stretch.

After another Lauenstein kill, Nichols won four consecutive points, making two kills and two blocks to help the Nittany Lions take a three-point lead. After a service error by Lauenstein, Finley Krystkowiak made the first three kills of her career to put Penn State on the verge of victory with a 19-14 lead.

Unlike the first two sets, UConn didn’t put up much of a fight in the closing stages. Penn State went on a three-point run to close within two of winning the match, and clinched the victory with a kill from Caroline Jurevicius to grab their first win of the year.

Up next

Penn State will play a doubleheader at Rec Hall against High Point and Hofstra on Sunday, with the matches set for 10 a.m. and 6 p.m., respectively. Both matchups can be streamed on B1G+.

title: DJ Diesel lit up LightsUP | 'I’m definitely coming back, Penn State'
author: Sarah Price | The Daily Collegian
description:
Students gathered on the HUB-Robeson Center’s lawn for Penn State’s annual free music festival, LightsUP Friday night in celebration of the first week of classes.

Run by the Student Programming Association (SPA) and Movin’ On as part of “Welcome Week,” the LightsUP festivities started at 5 p.m.

The event was free to attend, with special activities available to students around the HUB lawn such as face painting, henna, airbrush hats and even a mechanical surfboard. A Kona Ice truck also provided sweet shaved ice treats to cool attendees down.

Student performers, Waterfowl Festival Band and Spencer Graham kicked the night off and set the mood with some feel-good music, followed by DJ Flatman who played remixes of iconic songs like “Y.M.C.A.” by Village People.

According to Abby Wypych, the first few performers were enjoyable and quite impressive, especially considering they were students like herself.

“They (Waterfowl) surprised me because I saw it was student bands and I was like, ‘woah,’” Wypych, a third-year studying animal science, said.

After the student performers, Between Friends, a sibling duo, was the opening act for the highly anticipated headliner.

“It was really different from the DJing that was happening,” Naomi Michaels, a first-year studying kinesiology, said.

In the middle of their set, though, Between Friends left the stage due to a “We want Shaq,” chant circulating over a group in the crowd.

“Honestly, it was just super unexpected, but I guess they need to be respected too,” Lydia Laing, a first-year studying biomedical engineering, said in response to the duo's abrupt exit.

Michaels also commented on the sudden departure of the sibling duo, noting how confusing the situation was.

“I was surprised,” Michaels said. “I understood that it's disrespectful, but I feel like that’s just a part of entertainment.”

Shortly after Between Friends’ exit, DJ Diesel, widely known as Shaquille O’Neal, finally took the stage. Although he may be known more famously as a former NBA player for teams like the Los Angeles Lakers and the Orlando Magic, that didn't stop him from hyping up the crowd and playing his custom beats.

Unknown to many attendees, Shaq has been DJing under the name DJ Diesel since 2015.

“We didn’t know until we saw the advertisement for this, and we were like ‘who’s DJ Diesel?’” Wypych said.

Nonetheless, Penn State showed up ready to hear dubstep and electronic sounds on the HUB lawn from DJ Diesel.

Shaq’s large presence was felt immediately after he took the stage. Throughout his performance, numerous girls had the opportunity to be on stage with him, and he even had them sing a few lyrics.

“Put those phones away, it’s time to party,” Shaq said.

Shaq had the crowd singing along to his remixes of throwback songs such as “Livin’ on a Prayer” by Bon Jovi, “Don’t Stop Believin'” by Journey and “(I Just) Died in Your Arms” by Cutting Crew.

“I’m loving Shaq so far,” Olivia Bobber, a first-year in the Division of Undergraduate Studies, said. “I love his music, I love his mixes and it’s a really good vibe.”

Jackson Watters, a first-year studying finance, agreed with this sentiment and thoroughly enjoyed the 7-foot-1 celebrity's performance.

“I’m very excited about Shaq being here,” Watters said. “We’re vibing with it.”

The crowd was enthusiastic when Shaq remixed popular songs like “Mo Bamba” by Sheck Wes and “No Hands” by Waka Flocka Flame (feat. Wale & Roscoe Dash).

“I was not expecting to see this from Shaq, but I love to see it,” Janet Pajaziti, a first-year in the Division of Undergraduate Studies, said.

At one point, the Nittany Lion joined Shaq onstage during a remix of the song “Last Friday Night” by Katy Perry.

Shaq was enjoying Penn State just as much as the students, yelling “Ohio State sucks,” and even getting the crowd to chant it back. Toward the end of his set, Shaq even made a promise to students.

“I’m definitely coming back, Penn State,” Shaq said.

Despite all of the excitement and engagement from the crowd, DJ Diesel’s set ended unexpectedly due to technical issues. However, it was no doubt a night to remember for many who attended.

title: ‘It’s a special opportunity’ | Matt Campbell, Nittany Lions host 1st Victory Day at Penn State
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Blue Band, the cheer team, the Lionettes and the Nittany Lion all took the field to perform the regularly scheduled pregame festivities ahead of a Penn State game on Friday afternoon at Beaver Stadium.

However, the players themselves weren’t the stars of the show. This time, at Penn State’s first-annual Victory Day, underprivileged children with disabilities were given the opportunity to experience playing football, run drills and score a rushing touchdown.

True to the event’s name, the children even got to ring the Victory Bell at the end of the night.

“What a great night for our community, for our kids,” Matt Campbell said after Victory Day. “This world is about giving back and making a difference, and to be able to do that tonight, and be able to be with so many great families and young people that may never get the opportunity to play the game of football — it's a special opportunity for us.”

Campbell originally learned about Victory Day at a high school football camp in Michigan from Aaron Segedi, a coach at Trenton High School.

Since then, Campbell brought the event to his first head coaching job at Toledo, then popularized it at Iowa State before continuing it in Happy Valley.

Cooper Cousins, already beloved by the local community for his involvement with THON and Team IMPACT, a nonprofit organization that pairs an ill or disabled child with a collegiate athlete, said that the purpose of Victory Day “blends great” with the Penn State character.

“Why not do it on a night like this with the band, the cheer team, the Lionettes, the whole community around to give these kids an opportunity to feel what a touchdown feels like,” Cousins said. “It's not even just cool for them, it's cool for us to be able to experience something like that.”

Campbell emphasized how the event is about “putting things into perspective,” and said he believes that in the heat of the season, people can lose a sense of what is important to humanity.

Not only did Campbell claim the event was a great way to give back to the community, but also a way to give his players a night to “lean back on” as the team prepares for the season.

Victory Day was painted in the smiles and laughter of the children, their parents and the players that accompanied those families throughout the hour spent playing at Beaver Stadium.

“It's the best day of the year for me to get back to these kids to see a smile on their face,” Rocco Becht said. “It's truly the best thing in the world. As you can hear, it's the best day for them as well. We're just glad to be here and put a smile on these kids' faces.

As for the growth of the event at Penn State going forward, Campbell said that he doesn’t want the event to become a “popularity contest.” Instead, he wants the event to stay true to its goal of touching the lives of families in the community and grow naturally from there.

“This isn't trying to sell our program to anybody,” Campbell said. “This is to make a difference in the lives of other people, and to be honest with you, the more people we can make a difference in their lives, the better this opportunity is, and the more special this day becomes.”

title: Caden Grabfelder plays villain in return to Jeffrey Field as Penn State men’s soccer falls to Pitt
author: Elliott Inscho | Sports Editor
description:
Even after playing in 49 games over three seasons for Penn State, Caden Grabfelder was serenaded with chants of “traitor” by the Park Avenue Army as he entered the pitch in his return to Jeffrey Field.

The student section, featuring some members costumed as both a banana and cow, echoed the affront at the Pitt midfielder every time he absorbed a pass on Friday night.

Grabfelder had the last laugh. The senior midfielder converted a penalty to take the lead in the first half and spark the Panthers’ physical 2-1 victory.

“It was difficult, but at the end of the day we have to look at ourselves,” Amadou Kone, Penn State’s lone goalscorer, said. “We had some mistakes in the first half that we could have done better. Same thing in the second half. It's just about correcting those mistakes and going forward with that.”

The match got off to a pedestrian start until the sixth minute, when Kone beat his defender and seemed to have a lane towards the net, but was called for a foul after the referee deemed he pushed his opponent to the turf.

It was part of an early trend for the Nittany Lions, as they were called for five in the opening eight minutes, compared to Pitt’s none. The fifth, committed by Toby Grant, led to the best chance of the early minutes, as the Panthers’ free kick forced a punch from goaltender Daniel Peluffo-Wise.

Pitt upped the pressure on offense. Cannon Scretchen delivered a dangerous cross that was fired into Peluffo-Wise’s chest. Penn State got the Panthers out of their half, but the team from the east still controlled a lion’s share of possession as the 22-minute mark approached.

Penn State notched its first shot-on-goal of the match when Fielding won the ball off of Grabfelder and passed to Morgan Marshall, who fired a low drive towards the bottom-right corner of the net, but Pitt goaltender Jack Moxom pushed it away.

Moxom was called upon again when he punched away a long cross into the box, taking out Sheridan McNish in the process, to force associate head coach Brad Cole to sub him off for Nehan Hasan.

Cole served as the blue and white’s leader on Friday after head coach Rob Dow was shown a red card in Penn State’s preceding match against Missouri State.

“There's obviously an added responsibility,” Cole said on his role Friday night. “But every decision that we make is always discussed within the staff, and we had a plan coming in that we followed. [I] wasn't thinking about it too much.”

The Nittany Lions got another chance when Kone played Beckham Brown through with a lobbed ball. He sent it wide.

Pitt earned its penalty after the referee's initial no-call was overturned to a foul in the box.

Grabfelder grabbed the ball and stepped up to the penalty spot. A chorus of jeers rained down from a strong crowd in Happy Valley, but he remained composed and dinked his shot into the right side of the net.

After being heckled all evening, he returned fire to the student section, cupping his ear and rubbing the Pitt crest on his royal-blue jersey as he was engulfed by his teammates.

“They weren't creating high quality chances, and then obviously a penalty kind of changed the game,” Cole said. “We showed a lot of resilience to come back. At halftime, we were really happy with how things went. We thought we could pressure them a bit more, [and] in the second half we did.”

Penn State had a chance to answer back, as Grant McIntosh had space to shoot just outside the box, but he fired the ball directly into a defender.

Kone drew the Nittany Lions equal in the 38th minute, finding himself open and chipping a ball past Maxom. His second score and third goal involvement of the season inspired more offense from his squad, as they held possession in the attacking half in the minutes to follow.

“It's just my teammates putting me in positions to be successful,” Kone said about his early-season success. They have full trust in me, full confidence. They put me in the right positions, and it's just about me executing.”

Another almost-deadly chance came in the dying moments of the first half, when a ball delivered from nearly the midfield circle found McNish’s head, but he couldn’t deliver with sufficient enough power to find the nylon.

The second frame began similarly to the first, with both squads unable to get much going. Pitt midfielder Miguel Bertran took a long shot in the 53rd minute that sailed wide of the net.

Just over a minute later, Anders Bordoy fired a cross that took three deflections, two off Penn State players and the final off the post, before settling in the net. The score marked Bordoy’s first career goal and thrust the Panthers into the lead.

In the 63rd minute, Kone received the first card of the match, a yellow for pulling his opponent’s shirt. He won a foul in the 66th, but Brown’s ball towards goal bore no scoring chance.

Another yellow card was issued to Bertran in the 73rd minute, Pitt’s sixth foul in juxtaposition to No. 15 for the blue and white. On the ensuing free kick, the Nittany Lions delivered a ball into the box that caused some bodies to fall.

It warranted a challenge from Cole, but the reviewed video didn’t result in a penalty kick. Yet another yellow was delivered to Logan Oliver on a more harsh challenge from behind that might’ve been on another day.

As tensions continued to rise, Grabfelder saw a yellow card of his own in the 88th minute on yet another hard challenge by the Panthers. With just under ten minutes to play, there was a lengthy delay after midfielder Peter Doran went down with an injury.

Penn State’s fouls eclipsed 20 with less than five minutes to play in the match. With seconds draining from the clock, Grabfelder almost bagged a second goal with a curling shot on net, but Peluffo-Wise pushed it away at the last second.

The Nittany Lions crept past midfield and further into the offensive zone, and got a final scoring chance in the box, but Joseph Sheridan’s shot sailed wide to seal the defeat.

Up next

Penn State will stay home for another nonconference meeting, as they’ll face off with Bucknell on Tuesday. Kickoff is set for 7 p.m. from Jeffrey Field.

“We'll certainly be ready,” Cole said. “They also played Pittsburgh in their last match, so we've already watched them. They're a tough opponent, but we’ve just got to rest and rebound and have a good plan.”

title: Penn State urges community caution amid measles outbreak after 15 cases reported in Centre County
author: Neel Ved | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State officials issued a release on Thursday encouraging community members to exercise caution and take preventative steps against measles, a highly-contagious disease.

As of Friday, there were 460 reported measles cases in Pennsylvania this year, including two deaths, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health measles dashboard. These cases span 31 counties, with Centre County reporting 15 cases.

This week, Centre County’s reported cases were double the amount from last week.

According to the release, there are currently no confirmed cases at University Park or other Penn State campuses. However, 10 campuses are located in counties with confirmed cases.

Measles is spread through the air when an infected individual coughs or sneezes. The virus remains in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, though sometimes it can take up to 21 days.

The rash typically appears two to four days after the onset of fever. A person with measles is deemed contagious starting four days before through four days after the rash appears.

Penn State requires any incoming student to have two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. Students are advised to contact UHS or their primary care provider if they’re unsure of their immunity status to learn more about vaccination opportunities.

If students believe they have developed measles symptoms or were exposed to the virus, they’re advised to call the UHS Advice Nurse at 814-865-4847, before going to the Student Health Center.

title: Penn State field hockey begins play under coach Hannah Prince, suffers overtime loss to No. 5 Virginia
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
Hannah Prince will have to wait a little longer to get her first win as a member of the blue and white.

Penn State began its 2026 season, ushering in the coach Prince era in front of a sizable crowd against No. 5 Virginia. The blue and white ultimately couldn’t benefit from home turf, falling to the Cavaliers 4-3 in overtime.

Only 56 seconds in, the Nittany Lions fell behind for the first time under Prince. Penn State worked an early press off Virginia’s touch to start the game, and worked its opponent deep into its own half, but a deep-laid pass deflected off a blue and white stick, and worked past that effort.

With a majority of the defensive players out of position, Virginia passes easily found their way behind the defense for the Cavaliers’ Rylee Dennis to open the scoring.

The Nittany Lions’ fortunes improved from there despite Virginia holding possession in the shooting circle, with Hope Russo logging the first shot of the game for Penn State, but it aired over the net.

Penn State continued to press deep up the pitch, deploying extremely vocal play in its efforts, even including the phrase “Happy Valley” from players to dub one of its tactical switches. Still, after the first quarter, the blue and white trailed from the early leak in the defense with multiple long forward passes for the Nittany Lions without a receiver on the end of it.

The second quarter started with a much slower pace of play, as both sides were much more calculated and meticulous in possession. Penn State netminder Aby Deverka was forced to make her first save of the game roughly three minutes in, and her defense soon after failed to repay the favor.

At the five-minute mark, the Cavaliers found themselves with an odd-man rush, as Virginia played the ball to Riley Savage, who rocketed a shot with little to no chance of stopping.

The Nittany Lions regrouped after the goal and appeared reinvigorated, as they carried possession into Virginia’s half for the following minutes. The control allowed Josephine Purdy to fire a backhanded effort at the goal for Penn State’s second shot attempt, but it also skied the net.

With two minutes left in the half, the Nittany Lions threatened with a clear look off of a penalty corner. Still, the better of Ella Gaitan’s two shot attempts on the opportunity was denied on an acrobatic goalkeeping effort from Virginia. The Cavaliers utilized a much deeper rotation, using four more players over the half, with no field player playing the whole time. Prince, contrarily, used both Sienna Dunn and Morgan Snyder without a break.

Penn State started optimistically after the half, snuffed out the first Virginia attack with ease and countered with Dunn leading the charge, but the pass to Chloe Dhage went off her stick and out of play.

Just as the Nittany Lions’ missed chances began to stack, Virginia piled on via a rapid attack that netted a third goal courtesy of Livvy Barker. Last season’s leading scorer for the blue and white, Natalie Freeman soon after got her first attempt on goal of the game, but with a tight window on net she powered a shot that again missed the framework.

Penn State kept pushing, though. Russo again fired a shot at net, this time forcing a save, and a tight-strung pass in front of a point-blank Freeman in front of the net went offline, but the scoreless efforts kept the pressure up to end the quarter.

As time began to tick into the final quarter, the blue and white got more direct with its attacks, earning a penalty corner after three and a half minutes of play. The Nittany Lions’ efforts would finally be rewarded, as a deflection and scrum in front of the goal allowed Olivia Marthins to score an unassisted goal.

Crowding the shooting circle continued to be advantageous for Penn State, as Purdy soon cut in front of goal and played a pass to Gaitan that she converted, cutting the score to 3-2. Two minutes later, it would be tied, as Dunn dangled past the Cavaliers’ defenders to find Dhage for a dribbling tap-in.

With all going in Penn State’s favor, it had to deal with its first bit of major adversity in the quarter with a Virginia penalty corner with four minutes remaining. Still, Deverka padded away the shot attempt to keep it even.

The Cavaliers got another penalty corner opportunity, but a pair of stick deflections, the latter from Deverka on a heroic diving effort, saved the chance. The save didn’t stop the pressure, as another penalty corner resulted after a review, yet the effort into the circle was flubbed and Penn State took it into overtime.

The Nittany Lions threatened within the first minute of overtime when the Virginia netminder was forced to kick away a ball right at her feet, as the Penn State defense silenced the Cavaliers' early attacks.

That tide began to change as Virginia threatened with control and physicality, even knocking a pair of Nittany Lions to the ground briefly. That would be a sign of what was to come; the Cavaliers soon played a penalty corner to the edge of the circle to star Mia Abello, who fired a shot which found the back of the net to end the game.

Up Next

The Nittany Lions conclude their August competition with Sunday’s game against Lock Haven slated for noon.

title: Position preview | Penn State’s OL offers mixed bag of experience, youth
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s offensive line is a tale of two stories ahead of the 2026 season.

Only Anthony Donkoh, Trevor Buhr and Brock Riker have been starters for more than two games, while the other two players projected on the front five have not.

Here’s how Ryan Clanton’s offensive line is shaping up this season.

Returning starters

Of Penn State’s five projected starting offensive linemen, three of them are returning Nittany Lions from past seasons. But all three have varying experiences in Happy Valley.

Cooper Cousins was the first player to announce that he’d remain at Penn State in the wake of the Pinstripe Bowl, citing that playing for the university had always been his goal and that he’d stay loyal through it all.

Cousins is slated to start at right guard after spending the past two years seeing time on the field as a role player bouncing around the line. In his career, he’s made two starts — both last season — and only missed out on a single game due to injury.

Lining up next to him at right tackle, Donkoh has been considerably praised by Matt Campbell following his return from an undisclosed medical procedure that kept him off the field this spring, per Mark Brennan of 247Sports. The redshirt junior is the most experienced on the line in terms of starting games, making 21 starts in 28 games played.

“I have that experience and have the knowledge to be able to give back to them, and that's what I'm trying to do now,” Donkoh said on Aug. 7. “That's my role, trying to be able to give back, to be able to raise everybody up and get them up to speed before they have their you know first game time experience.

As the starting right tackle in 2024, Donkoh drew national attention despite suffering a season-ending injury against Minnesota in November, earning an All-Big Ten honorable mention and a spot as a semifinalist on the Shaun Alexander Freshman of the Year Award list.

Redshirt freshman Malachi Goodman has garnered a lot of attention throughout the offseason despite the fact that he hasn’t made his collegiate debut yet. He’s projected to protect Rocco Becht’s blindside at left tackle, inheriting the role from Drew Shelton.

Goodman, a former 4-star recruit, was Penn State’s top signee in the Class of 2025 after graduating high school as the No. 2 player out of New Jersey and the No. 9 offensive lineman in the nation, per 247Sports composite.

“Malachi, good news, is one of the most talented guys I've ever seen with my own two eyes,” offensive coordinator Taylor Mouser said in April.

Impactful transfers

The other two members of the potential starting lineup are transfers with different backgrounds.

Trevor Buhr, who’ll likely line up next to Goodman at left guard, is the sole projected starting Iowa State transfer on the line. He’s had meaningful starting experience with the Cyclones, making 12 starts in 21 games played. Last season, Buhr was named an All-Big 12 honorable mention.

Texas State transfer Brock Riker will likely round out the starting line at center. He had a standout redshirt freshman campaign with the Bobcats, starting all 12 games in 2025 and being named a second-team Freshman All-American by The Athletic.

Riker was one of the first players that stuck out to Campbell out of the transfer portal, he said on Tuesday, because of his experience with in-game reps. Additionally, Campbell noted that Riker has put on upwards of 30 pounds this offseason, reaching around the 305-pound mark, transforming his physique to play in the Big Ten.

“Not only (Riker’s) experience was positive, but the way he played,” Campbell said. “Then you research, man, he was great on the weightlifting team, he was a great wrestler. How he was built when he came, and we just felt like this guy's got a chance to be a really special football player.”

Battling positional depth

The most notable position battles at this point include the left tackle and the center spot, for which Campbell has expressed his excitement for the projected starters, but also emphasized that everyone is still in an “earn it position.”

At left tackle, redshirt sophomore Garrett Sexton and redshirt freshman Owen Aliciene are in the mix. Sexton is the more seasoned option, having appeared in all 13 games last year, while Aliciene only appeared in one during his true freshman season.

Redshirt senior Dominic Rulli — a former walk-on — is currently the projected backup center, having appeared in every game for the past three seasons on special teams. He made his first collegiate start at center in the Pinstripe Bowl.

Rulli was initially the favorite for the job, but part of the reason why Riker is now in the lead is due to an injury that forced Rulli to miss spring ball, giving Riker all of the first-team reps.

title: No. 10 Penn State women’s volleyball falls to No. 11 SMU in Spikes Under the Lights opener
author: Elliott Inscho | Sports Editor
description:
Penn State headed to Arlington to open its season in a high-profile exhibition tournament, and its time in AT&T Stadium ended in a way that’s all-too familiar for the Dallas Cowboys’ faithful.

Matched up against a No. 11 SMU squad that sat just a single slot below them in the AVCA preseason poll, the No. 10 Nittany Lions fell in a two-set sweep to open the year on the wrong foot.

After No. 1 Nebraska also defeated No. 17 Florida in two hotly-contested sets to begin the evening, it was finally time for the Nittany Lions to make their 2026 debut.

SMU started the exhibition off hot, winning back-to-back points before Whitney Lauenstein got Penn State on the board with a smooth tap that lobbed over the net and onto the jet-black court.

After the Mustangs got another point, Lauenstein received a pass from Kennedy Martin and powered the ball to the back line, barely landing in bounds. Alexis Stucky’s first ace in the blue and white brought things level at three points each.

The squads went back-and-forth to follow, tying again at 6-6 not long after. SMU capped a four-point run, going up a pair of points, but the blue and white scored two unanswered to tie things up yet again.

SMU led 11-9 at the media timeout, and won the next point before a service error finally got Penn State back on the board. After an already hot start, Lauenstein brought the blue and white back within one with an emphatic spike.

For the Mustangs, Favor Anyanwu showed off her vertical in the middle with several high-flying leaps that fueled the Mustangs to a 15-12 lead late in the set. Two back-to-back blocks from the Nittany Lions forced SMU coach Sam Erger to take her first timeout of the match.

It didn’t help. Martin and Ryla Jones combined to block a Suli Davis spike and tie the set, but Davis got her revenge by winning the next point to put the Mustangs back on top.

A serve from Anyanwu was too much for Ava Falduto and Emmi Sellman to handle, leading Katie Schumacher-Cawley to call her first timeout down 18-16.

Schumacher-Cawley’s timeout had a juxtaposing effect to Erger’s, though, as Kennedy Martin scored consecutive kills to knot things back up again. After an SMU point and a long rally, she notched her fifth kill to level things at 19.

SMU earned another point after a high-level dig from libero Victoria Harris to reach the brink of set point, but a service ace kept the Nittany Lions alive.

The Mustangs reached set point again, but Lauenstein delivered to extend it further. SMU got yet another set-clinching opportunity on a Penn State service error, but a kill from Martin lengthened things even further.

On their third set point, SMU nearly fell victim to Lauenstein again, but she fired the ball just wide to post her first attacking error of the set and give the Mustangs a 24-22 victory in the opening frame.

SMU kept its momentum to begin the second set, jumping out to a 5-2 advantage, but a lengthy review reversed the fifth point in favor of the Nittany Lions and made the lead just a single point. Anyanwu got her fourth kill of the match to put the Mustangs up by a trio of points, but Martin answered back with one of her own.

After two straight points won by Penn State, the squads traded the next few points before Penn State thought it’d tied things up, but another review reversed that call as well. Coming out of the media timeout, Davis notched a kill to give the Mustangs a 12-10 lead.

SMU went up by three as the set continued on, but Haley Burgdorf finished a kill on a fourth-consecutive assist from Stucky, keeping things tight down the stretch.

The match’s competitiveness was a theme throughout, and the teams found themselves tied again at 15. Lauenstein’s tenth kill gave Penn State its first lead since the opening set and capped a 5-1 run before SMU drew level on the next point.

Davis reached double-digit kills to force another timeout from Schumacher-Cawley with the Mustangs holding an 18-17 advantage. Lauenstein was sharp all night, but an attack error put SMU on the brink of victory.

Martin fired a ball past the back line to inhibit match point, and it seemed as if Lauenstein did the same on the next point, but a review further extended the match. In SMU’s second attempt to end it, Davis made no mistake and delivered a strong swing to send Penn State home early.

title: Women's soccer coach Erica Dambach earns 300th Penn State win, thumps Bucknell
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions hosted the Bucknell Bison at Jeffrey Field at 7:30 pm on Thursday. Penn State bounced back after a 1-2 loss against West Virginia.

Coach Erica Dambach earned her 300th win in her career with the Nittany Lions after a dominant 5-0 win against the Bison.

“Overall, one of my top five nights of my career,” Dambach said. “I couldn’t even keep my emotions together, and then walking off of (the field), I think I'm even more emotional than I was before the game started, and that's saying a lot.”

Bucknell kicked off the match with possession of the ball in the Nittany Lions half, yet the white and blue defended their first offensive push well.

For the first five minutes of the game, both squads battled defensively, not allowing the opposing offenses to hold possession for long stints.

Penn State's first set piece of the match was a corner kick that was batted down by Bucknell’s goalkeeper, which she then collected.

A notable defensive stop came from defender Kayleigh Herr. A clearance attempt bounced off a Penn State defender and landed in the possession of a Bucknell attacker. Herr made a sliding tackle to stop a potential goal.

Penn State's attackers kept sending passes to teammates making runs, but the Bison defenders shielded them well.

Another mishandled goal kick by Penn State's defense almost led to a goal when Bucknell’s attack took several shots at the goal that were blocked near the goalline by both Mackenzie Gress and two defenders.

While their inability to track goalkicks was an early concern for the Nittany Lions, they were able to hold possession, leading to early corner kicks and shot attempts. When the defense didn’t make self-inflicted mistakes, the team controlled the match.

That control of the ball paid off when Paige Pasinski scored the opening goal of the game, slotting the ball into the bottom left corner of the goal after an assist from Aubrey Kulpa to take a 1-0 lead. The Nittany Lions methodically moved downfield by playing from the back, making runs, and finding the open man.

Bucknell’s defense played a low-line, waiting to pressurize the ball around midfield, but the white and blue handled the disruption well. Nittany Lion defenders passed back and forth until finding a midfielder making a run or sitting in space waiting to receive the ball.

Yet, the Bisons’ defense bent but didn’t break, defending various corner kicks and offensive pushes made by the Nittany Lions.

At around nine minutes left in the half, the white and blue defense played a bit sloppily in its defensive third. A poor clearance attempt led to a corner kick opportunity, in which a header sailed wide of the goal.

After the ball was cleared, Ellie Kocher received it around midfield, made a nice run down the left side, outpacing a defender in the process, before her shot went wide right.

With three minutes left, the Nittany Lions had all the momentum. A shot on goal outside the box led to a corner kick for the white and blue. Paige Kalal sent the kick back post for Lily Burger, who headed the ball into the back of the net to head into halftime with a 2-0 lead.

Even with the lead, the Nittany Lions didn’t play a perfect brand of soccer.

“I thought the game was played on their terms in the second half,” Dambach said. It’s hard when teams are putting balls on top of you to then settle the game.”

Coach Dambach’s message at halftime was to return to their style of play, and that’s exactly what they did.

To begin the half, Bucknell played with more defenders back to stop Penn State from making runs in the middle of the field.

That didn’t stop the Nittany Lions from finding ways to get open, when a through ball was sent into the box and chased down by Kocher. The Bucknell goalie attempted to slide tackle Kocher, but clipped her legs instead, resulting in a penalty kick for the white and blue. Bucknell challenged the call but was unsuccessful.

Hannah Jordan’s penalty was saved, but the goalkeeper's failure to catch the ball resulted in a rebound back to Jordan and a goal to take a 3-0 lead in the first couple minutes of the second half.

Penn State began to dominate on both ends of the field. The Nittany Lion attack was firing on all cylinders with multiple shots on goal within a five-minute span, while the defense limited passes on their side of the field.

That trend continued with a goal from Aubrey Kulpa that hit the right post and bounced in for Kulpa’s second goal contribution of the night. A pass was sent in by Anna Babcock for her first career assist.

With 21 minutes left in the match, the white and blue kept making the game look easy. Another goal was scored by Kaelyn Wolfe on the right side of the box, which was assisted by Nicole Crane. The Nittany Lions took a commanding 5-0 lead.

The Nittany Lions can thank their defense for a portion of their second-half offensive success, as they’ve put an end to every attack that Bucknell has attempted to put together. The defense finished the game with something to show for it, as they earned their first clean sheet of the season.

“They held it down back there,” Aubrey Kulpa said. “They do their job, and they encourage us. They build out of the back and then we can do our job.”

title: Penn State notebook | Rob Dow talks men's soccer matchup against Pittsburgh
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
After an intense loss against Missouri State saw both sophomore defender Joe Buckley and coach Rob Dow ejected and sidelined for their upcoming match, the Nittany Lions will look to regain their confidence as they take on Pittsburgh in another nonconference matchup.

Both teams currently sit at 1-1, with the Panthers coming off a 3-1 win against Bucknell. With strong midfielders like Grayson Carter, Logan Oliver and ex-Nittany Lion Caden Grabfelder, Penn State will have to focus its efforts on keeping the ball and going against the Panthers' strong counterpress.

“Defensively, we must stay compact, not get stretched out,” Dow said. “They’re typically pretty good in possessing and balancing teams on the ball, but we’re excited.”

As the team tries to rebuild after finishing last in the Big Ten two years ago and losing all but three players from their previous season, coach Dow will rely on key returnee Amadou Kone.

“He’s a direct, fast, tenacious attacking player that can convert and create for sure,” Dow said. “But once he gets into space, that’s when he comes alive.”

Kone, who assisted the blue and white’s first and only goal against the Bears, will has an opportunity to continue his play, leaving enough space behind the wide back for him to attack the ball and get in a groove.

Dow will also have the likes of Nehan Hassan, one of the newest faces for the blue and white.

“He’s playing above his years; he’s a young player, but he doesn’t feel like a young player in the program,” Dow said. “When he picks up the ball, things happen. He can eliminate the first player, the second player, a top-tier player.”

Penn State also looks to play to their strengths during the match to compete against the Panthers' offensive plays, prioritizing the set piece.

“I think we’ll have the quality of advantage against Pitt on corners, on direct free kicks, Joe Sheridan’s vicious height, Toby Grant’s vertical jump, the onset of Bill Forester,” Dow said. “We're getting good service to those guys so that’ll be a big focus.”

With Dow being out, Brad Cole will fill in as interim coach during the match. A standout player himself in college, Cole has knowledge on and off the field, having worked under Dow in his previous role at Vermont.

“We have a tremendous amount of trust and respect for each other,” Dow said. “But he’ll do an amazing job in the program, probably better.”

title: Penn State men’s soccer presented with chance to bounce back against Pittsburgh
author: Luci Palacios | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State will look to bounce back from its first loss of the season when it hosts Pittsburgh at 7 p.m. Friday at Jeffrey Field.

The Nittany Lions enter the matchup 1-1 after opening the season with a 3-2 win over Mercyhurst before falling 3-1 to Missouri State on the road. Pittsburgh also holds a 1-1 record after losing 2-1 to then-No. 7 Maryland in its opener before responding with a 3-1 win over Bucknell.

Notably, a familiar face will return to Happy Valley in Friday’s matchup, this time representing the opposing team.

On July 28, former Nittany Lion star midfielder Caden Grabfelder transferred to Pittsburgh after three seasons with Penn State. Grabfelder appeared in 49 games during his time at Happy Valley, recording nine goals and nine assists before joining the Panthers.

Grabfelder was one of Penn State’s main contributors last season, starting 14 of 16 games and finishing with two goals and five assists. His move to Pittsburgh gives the Nittany Lions an early contest against a player who already knows the team and its home field well.

The Panthers are coming off a rough 6-7-5 season in 2025, while Penn State finished 5-8-4. Both teams have a chance to put those records behind them after getting their first wins of the new season.

Just as Pittsburgh rebounded with a two-goal win over Bucknell, Penn State looks for a similar response after its loss to Missouri State. The Nittany Lions took an early lead when senior midfielder Luca Sowinski scored his first collegiate goal in the 18th minute, with senior forward Amadou Kone earning his first collegiate assist on the play.

Missouri State tied the game before halftime and took control early in the second half, scoring just one minute after the break. The Bears added another goal from the penalty box in the 51st minute before things took a turn for the worse for the Nittany Lions.

Freshman Joe Buckley was sent off in the 56th minute after receiving his second yellow card of the match. Coach Rob Dow was also ejected later in the game after receiving a red card, meaning both he and Buckley will be unavailable against Pittsburgh.

The Nittany Lions will have to adjust without their coach and one of their defenders, but also have a chance to use Friday’s game as a reset. Penn State has historically controlled the series, holding a 24-9-4 record across 36 meetings with the Panthers.

However, Pittsburgh has had the upper hand in recent years, going 3-2-2 against the Nittany Lions since 2008. The Panthers won the most recent meeting, a 2-1 victory at Jeffrey Field in 2024.

With both teams sitting at 1-1, Friday’s matchup gives Penn State a chance to move back above .500 while facing a former teammate and a Pittsburgh team looking to build off its first win of the season.

title: Position preview | Penn State’s LBs bring depth to defense
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s linebacker room has a much different look entering this season.

After bringing in four players from Iowa State, retaining Tony Rojas and adding several younger players, linebacker is one of the deepest positions on the Nittany Lions’ roster this year, a stark contrast from last season when depth was thin.

Here’s a look at Penn State’s linebackers ahead of the 2026 season.

Starters

After his redshirt sophomore season was cut short due to a torn ACL, Tony Rojas announced his return for a fourth year to Happy Valley. He’s been a consistent starter the last two years and made a major impact on the field during his healthy sophomore season.

Rojas’ breakout season came in 2024 when he recorded 58 tackles, six tackles for loss and a trio of interceptions — including a pick six against SMU in the first round of the College Football Playoff. He’s had to adapt to new defensive coordinator D’Anton Lynn’s scheme while rehabbing.

“I feel great,” Rojas said at local media day on Aug. 7. “Feels good to be back and can’t wait for the season.”

Taking the MIKE role and wearing the green dot is Kooper Ebel, who came over from Iowa State with Matt Campbell.

Ebel has also been a full-time starter the last two seasons, but has been more effective in run defense than Rojas. He’s recorded 149 tackles, 14 tackles for loss and a pair of sacks over the past three years.

The third starter entering this season will be another one of Campbell’s former products. Cael Brezina slowly made a name for himself through two seasons at Iowa State, but has had even more success this offseason.

When discussing Brezina’s work during fall camp, Campbell said his performance has been “the best football he’s seen Cael Brezina play, maybe in his career.”

Role players

Caleb Bacon started all 12 games for Iowa State last season, with many thinking he’d see a similar role with the Nittany Lions.

However, Campbell discussed during local media day a potential move to defensive end for the Iowa State transfer, as Bacon said “I think I'm really just ready for whatever.”

Bacon will likely split time between both positions after a standout redshirt junior year with the Cyclones, where he recorded 68 tackles, 9.5 tackles for loss and three sacks.

Sophomore Alex Tatsch — one of the few returners to Penn State’s linebacker room — played in six games and recorded 14 tackles during his true freshman campaign.

Tatsch picked up an injury before the Pinstripe Bowl that left him sidelined much of the offseason. However, Campbell said on Aug. 13 that he’s trending positively through recovery, but didn’t indicate whether he’d be available for Week 1.

Depth pieces

The Nittany Lions have many young players with little to no collegiate playing experience who could provide depth to this year’s linebacker room if needed.

Redshirt freshman Cam Smith is the most talked about of those remaining six linebackers on Penn State’s squad, as Campbell said on Aug. 25 that he’s “gotten better every day.”

John Klosterman is one of the more veteran linebackers on the team after four seasons at Iowa State, but he’s only played in 24 games and recorded 18 tackles during his career.

Sophomore Chris Fileppo comes from West Virginia, where he made one start and an additional 11 appearances as a true freshman.

The Nittany Lions have three additional freshmen linebackers in Keian Kaiser, Josh Banks and Evan Wolff who may see the field as a result of redshirt seasons ultimately being eliminated.

title: Penn State field hockey opens season hosting Virginia, Lock Haven
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Hannah Prince era in Happy Valley is looming with Penn State’s season right around the corner. The team will start the season in State College, playing a pair of Games against Virginia on Thursday and Lock Haven on Sunday.

Prince comes into the Nittany Lions head coaching job with top-notch experience at the collegiate Level. As coach of St Joseph's, she led the team to a historic National Championship appearance in 2024 and also registered a 64-24 record across her four seasons with the Red Hawks, collecting NCAA tournament appearances in each of those years. In her last season, she guided St Joseph’s to its fifth straight Atlantic 10 championship title. Prince has an opportunity to bring this experience to a Penn State team that struggled during the 2025 season.

The Nittany Lions are led by senior midfielder Natalie Freeman. The Ellicott City, Maryland, native, is expected to be Penn State’s primary goal scorer in 2026 after a stellar 2025 season in which she notched 19 points in 17 matches. Over her career, Freeman logged a total of 26 points in 32 games.

Virginia

In 31 all-time meetings against the Cavaliers, Penn State leads the series 21-11, but the Cavaliers have won the last two matchups, with the most recent meeting resulting in a 5-1 Virginia win in 2025. Last season was a good one for the Cavaliers, going 16-3, losing in the ACC Championship.

Senior breakout Mia Abello is Virginia’s best attacking threat, putting up 20 points in 19 games played en route to All ACC-First Team honors in 2025. Last year, Abello had one assist against Penn State and enters again as a threat for the blue and white defense.

The Cavaliers enter Happy Valley as one of the nation's top contenders, with the No. 5 spot in the preseason NFHCA Poll, as it poses an immediate test for Prince’s squad to jump right into the fire.

Virginia is also an extremely different squad from last season, with seven true freshmen, four of whom were ranked inside the nation's top-50 in the class, proving the Cavaliers carry a scary mix of both youth and veteran talent.

Lock Haven

To round out the weekend, Lock Haven comes to State College to take on the Nittany Lions in a 46th all-time matchup where the blue and white leads the series 20-22-3.

The last time these two teams matched up in 2025, Penn State won in an 8-0 thrashing where Freeman and Ella Jennes led the charge with the pair combining for five goals.

Lock Haven had a season to forget in 2025, going 2-16. With such a disappointing result on the pitch, the Bald Eagles appointed Valerie Clarke as the new head coach in May. The new boss arrives at Lock Haven after a successful tenure with Converse University, where Clarke had coached since 2018.

At Converse, Clarke earned numerous accolades, including back-to-back South Atlantic Conference Tournament Championships in 2021 and 2022, which helped her earn SAC Coach of the Year honors.

The new appointments go head-to-head directly in their second games with their new squads, with Clarke making her away debut with Lock Haven.

title: Penn State’s women’s volleyball follows Spikes Under the Lights with Penn State Invitational
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
After its appearance in Spikes Under the Lights, Penn State women’s volleyball is kicking off its nonconference play in the Penn State Invitational on Saturday. The Nittany Lions will play three matches throughout the weekend, against UConn, Hofstra and High Point.

Coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley's squad closed its last season in round two of the NCAA Tournament, after being swept by the Texas Longhorns — a bit of a letdown, as the blue and white were the previous reigning champions after its triumphant run in 2024, going 35-2.

Penn State has a powerful duo at its forefront this year. Florida transfers Alexis Stucky and Kennedy Martin form a powerful setter and right-side tag team. Stucky is beginning her first season with the Nittany Lions this year, but Martin transferred to Penn State prior to the 2025 season.

On Saturday, the Nittany Lions will face off against the UConn Huskies. The two teams have only seen each other nine times and only once this millennium, when Penn State won in a sweep in 2022.

UConn has reinforcements all over the court, with a large veteran presence in the front row and a stable libero in the back.

Senior Grace Maria has been at UConn since her freshman year. As a first-year, she appeared in 26 matches. After that, she constantly appeared in every game of her sophomore and junior seasons and is expected to lead in the front again this year.

She was named to the Bearcat Classic All-Tournament Team and totaled 146 kills, 36 aces, 71 blocks and 170 digs on the season.

Along with Maria, senior Isabella Suhy adds reinforcement to the Husky back line. As libero, Suhy totaled 85 digs last year, and 245 digs in her UConn career thus far. Just last season in the Huskies' match against Seton Hall, she reached a season high of 16 digs.

On Sunday, Penn State will play two matches: one at 10 a.m. and one at 6 p.m. The blue and white will first face off against High Point.

High Point and Penn State have never met in program history.

The Panthers haven’t altered a majority of its roster. They are holding onto 10 players and adding five new freshmen and one Virginia Tech transfer. Since around 90% of the roster played together last season, their chemistry is at the core of their offense.

Penn State will conclude its three-match weekend at 6 p.m. Sunday against the Hofstra Pride. In program history, the two teams have met nine times, but not in recent years. Their latest match was in 2019, where Penn State won 3-0.

The Pride are led by CAA honorees Beatriz Braga and Constanza Perez Sain. Braga was named CAA Preseason Player of the Year on August 19th and both players were named to the Preseason All-CAA Team.

While each team poses its own defensive threats, offensive duos and veteran experience, Penn State is favored in each match. They are currently ranked No. 10 in the NCAA’s AVCA rankings, whereas the other three are not in the Top 25.

title: A glance at Penn State women’s volleyball’s transfer, recruiting newcomers for the 2026 season
author: Lily Dorf | The Daily Collegian
description:
As the 2026 Women’s Volleyball season begins on Thursday, new faces will be taking the court as Nittany Lions. The team welcomed seven new athletes this year, including four freshman recruits and three transfers.

Here’s a brief overview of each player.

Freshman Recruits

Kendall Northern

Kendall Northern is a 6-foot-1 middle blocker from Cincinnati, who was ranked nationally as Prep Dig’s No. 13 high school recruit in the class of 2026.

In her senior year, she won Gatorade 2025-2026 Player of the Year with 601 kills and 273 digs. She played on Summit Country Day High School’s varsity team all four years, racking up 1,236 kills and 538 digs by the end of her high school career.

Danielle Whitmire

Another recruit stepping onto the court is 6-foot-2 setter Whitmire from Celina, Texas.

She arrives in Happy Valley as Penn State’s highest-rated freshman via Dig Prep, standing at No. 4 nationally. Whitmire played for Walnut Grove High School as well as Texas Advantage Volleyball Club.

Whitmire was on Walnut Grove’s varsity team all four years, racking up 1,100 kills and an 89.9 percent serving percentage. Most notably, she played for USAVolleyball’s 2025 girls U19 (Under 19) national team.

Haley Burgdorf

Joining Northern and Whitmire this season is 6-foot outside hitter Burgdorf, hailing from St. Charles, Illinois.

Burgdorf is ranked No. 29 nationally for the 2026 season via Prep Dig. During her high school career, Burgdorf racked up a combined 695 kills and 309 digs during her freshman and senior years on varsity. She was named Illinois’ Gatorade’s 2025-2026 Player of the Year and Under Armor’s All-American Volleyball Team in 2025.

Finley Krystkowiak

The final commit for the Penn State Nittany Lions is 6-foot-4 outside hitter Krystkowiak.

She was Prep Dig’s No. 10 recruit and hails from San Diego, California. Krystkowiak previously played for Torrey Pines High School and Wave Volleyball Club. During her high school career, Krystkowiak racked up 1,344 kills and 922 digs during her four years on varsity.

Krystkowiak comes from an all-star family, with twin sister Samantha Krystkowiak playing beach volleyball for Stanford University, and father Larry Krystkowiak playing in the NBA, most notably with the Chicago Bulls.

The newcomers will make their debut at Spikes Under the Light in Arlington, Texas on Aug. 27.

Transfers

Alexis Stucky

Along with the incoming recruits, 6-foot-2 setter Stucky will be joining the Nittany Lions. Stucky is a redshirt senior from Laramie, Wyoming, and transferred in from Florida.

Stucky and star teammate Kennedy Martin both previously played for the Gators and are reunited once again as teammates. Stucky played four seasons with Florida, where she totaled 626 digs, 80 aces, 3,047 assists and 167 total blocks.

Ryla Jones

The next transfer is 6-foot-2 middle blocker Jones. She’s a junior from Oxon Hill, Maryland, who transferred from Pittsburgh.

Jones played two seasons as a Panther, totaling 230 kills, 212 total blocks and 22 assists across 62 matches. During her debut year, Jones was named to the All-ACC Freshman Team.

Whitney Lauenstein

The last transfer of the season is 6-foot-2 outside hitter Lauenstein from Waverly, Nebraska. Lauenstein is a graduate student who transferred from Texas, totaling 36 kills, 89 total attacks, 15 total blocks and 12 digs across her previous two seasons.

Lauenstein also played for Nebraska her freshman and sophomore years, totaling 359 kills, 953 total attacks, 123 digs and 136 total blocks.

title: Former Penn State RB Miles Sanders arrested for driving under the influence
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor

Former Penn State running back Miles Sanders was arrested June 8 in Churchill Borough near Pittsburgh for driving under the influence, according to court documents.

Sanders was charged with driving under the influence of alcohol or a controlled substance and careless driving. His preliminary hearing is set for Oct. 28.

Sanders played for the Nittany Lions from 2016-18, where he became the 45th player in Penn State history to rush for over 1,000 yards and was a second-team All-Big Ten selection in 2018.

The Pittsburgh native was drafted in the second round of the 2018 NFL Draft to the in-state Philadelphia Eagles. Sanders spent four years with the Eagles before spending 2023-24 with the Carolina Panthers.

title: Penn State DT Siale Taupaki taking initiative, guiding defensive line
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
In order to hold up against a Big Ten offense, Penn State’s defensive line must be the best it can possibly be. Defensive tackle Siale Taupaki knows this all too well after spending the past seven seasons at UCLA before becoming a Nittany Lion.

Having that experience under his belt has given him enough wisdom to act as the defensive line’s mentor and role model. Taupaki has taken it upon himself to guide both his fellow veterans and the younger generation to get the whole unit on the same page.

Taupaki has been setting up one-on-one meetings as a way of keeping people accountable and to leave no doubt in anyone’s mind about what to do and how to do it. It’s also a way to keep himself in the mix because regardless of his age, he’s still in a position to learn from anyone on the roster.

“I believe that one-on-one meetings with each of the players is beneficial because you get to actually pick and see where they're coming from, how they dissect the information that they see on the field,” Taupaki said on Tuesday. “After we're done with the field, we come back together and I say ‘Shoot it to me, what do you see? How can I help? How do you play the game?’”

While Taupaki has an instinctive urge to lead, he doesn’t credit that as a desire to coach in the future. For him, it’s just baked into his nature. He said that from a young age, he’s always taken initiative in these situations purely of his own accord.

It’s also a culmination of his observations from “being around great people” and watching those individuals play football in their own ways and with their own unique styles.

“Everybody learns in a different way,” Taupaki said. “Some guys are better at being in the meeting room versus some guys who are better on the field, going through it, walk-through, seeing it for themselves. So I try to learn everyone because that's who I am too.”

Despite not being interested in coaching at this time, Taupaki’s words about how great of a teacher D’Anton Lynn is closely echoed the description that he gave himself.

“With Lynn, there's certain things that he wants done, but then his doors are always open for us to come up to find the little knicks and knacks that we can fix,” Taupaki said. “That's one thing that I truly like because if you’ve ever been with someone that they like stuff a certain way, you try to go in and talk to them, but they don't want to. It's different with Lynn.”

Ahead of his first and only season at Penn State, Taupaki’s message was clear. Each individual defensive player has to be completely ready at all times.

“Between now and gameday, I believe that what I need to succeed personally is understanding, going towards that game, that each of my guys are gonna do their job,” Taupaki said. “If you stay prepared, you'll be ready. But until then, I want to make sure that the guys and I are all on the same page fundamentally, technically, communicating. I want to be able to have that mindset. Other than that, let's just play ball.”

title: No. 10 Penn State women’s volleyball set to open season in Spikes Under the Lights tournament in Dallas
author: Elliott Inscho | Sports Editor
description:
Penn State’s 2026 campaign starts on one of the biggest stages that collegiate women’s volleyball has ever been played on.

The Nittany Lions are heading to Arlington, Texas, where they’ll participate in the Spikes Under the Lights tournament at AT&T Stadium, the home of the Dallas Cowboys.

Katie Schumacher-Cawley’s squad will have a chance to set the tone for the year after being eliminated by No. 3 Texas in the NCAA second round to close last season. Here’s everything you need to know for the historic event in the Lone Star State.

The format

Spikes Under the Lights will see four preeminent women’s volleyball teams take to the court on national television, although the matches will officially go down as best-of-three-set exhibitions.

The first serve of the night will come in the bracket’s opening match, being played between Nebraska and Florida at 8:00 p.m. Then, the Nittany Lions will take to the court at 9:00 p.m. for their season debut against SMU.

After those matches conclude, the winners will meet for the tournament championship at 10:00 p.m.

The participants

Penn State will be thrown directly into the fire to begin the season, as all of the squads in the four-team tournament were ranked in the AVCA preseason poll.

SMU placed No. 11 to start the year, one spot below the blue and white. Spikes Under the Lights won’t be the first on-court action of the year for the Mustangs, though.

They opened their season on Sunday with a sweep of No. 8 Texas A&M as part of the AVCA First Serve tournament. Sophomore outside hitter Suli Davis led SMU with 15 kills in her first match as a Mustang after transferring from BYU.

On the other side of the bracket, Florida will provide a familiar challenge for Kennedy Martin and Alexis Stucky, who both began their career in Gainesville.

The Gators slotted in at No. 17 in the AVCA’s opening poll after posting a 16-12 record last season. Their season ended in the NCAA second round when they were swept by SMU, but Florida could potentially set up a rematch in the tournament championship if they can take down Nebraska.

It won’t be easy, though. Nebraska was ranked No. 1 overall to open the year, and received 57 out of 63 total first-place votes.

The Cornhuskers are led by middle blocker Andi Jackson, outside hitter Harper Murray and setter Bergen Reilly, who each earned unanimous All-Big Ten preseason honors.

The only other unanimous addition to that list? Kennedy Martin.

What’s at stake

A total of $1 million is to be awarded on Thursday night.

Each program will receive $200,000 for participating in the tournament, with an additional $200,000 going to the team that ultimately claims the championship. It’s the largest prize pool ever up for grabs in the history of women’s college sports.

Even though the matches won’t go on the teams’ official record, the high-level matchups will provide a strong opportunity to build momentum early in the season.

For the Nittany Lions, they’ll look to seize on that chance after losing 13 matches last season, the most in a single campaign for the blue and white since they lost 15 in 1982.

The “three-hour primetime event” will be broadcast on TBS starting at 8:00 p.m.

Over the last six seasons, the Bears finished first in the Ivy League regular season four times, showcasing their ability to dominate their conference. Brown will get the chance to showcase its skills this Sunday in the nearly two-decade-awaited rematch since the 2008 UConn Classic.

What to watch for Penn State

The Nittany Lions are still searching for their first regular season win and are hoping to do so in front of their fans.

title: Big Ten approves rule prohibiting former NFL players to join a team in the conference
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
The Big Ten athletic directors have unanimously approved a rule prohibiting any player from returning to a team in its conference that has played in the NFL. ESPN’s Pete Thamel first reported Tuesday morning that this rule was expected to be passed.

With this ruling, anyone who has declared for the NFL draft and did not withdraw, appeared on an NFL roster or signed a contract with a pro league cannot be on a Big Ten roster, per Thamel.

The SEC also approved a similar rule on Tuesday night, and the Big 12 is set to follow suit.

This comes in light of former college players from the 2022 recruiting class signing deals to return to college football after being waived or released by NFL teams. Specifically, former Ole Miss tight end Dae’Quan Wright had an agreement in place with Lane Kiffin and LSU after being waived by the Cleveland Browns.

Wright initially signed with the Philadelphia Eagles as an undrafted free agent before getting released and joining the Browns. He played in Cleveland’s preseason matchup against the Buffalo Bills on Aug. 22 despite entering the transfer portal two days earlier.

Multiple coaches in the Big Ten have spoken out against moves like Wright’s, including Oregon’s Dan Lanning and Ohio State’s Ryan Day.

“To think that we’re in a situation where we’re this late in the season and our rosters are not locked in is frustrating at the very least, but I’m not going to sit here and keep saying that,” Day told local reporters on Monday.

Day added that he had been in contact with Big Ten commissioner Tony Pettiti about potentially creating a rule against NFL players coming back to college. A day later, that idea became law within the conference.

The Big Ten was the first conference to take action on this situation, but the SEC shortly followed, and the ACC is set to discuss similar rules, per On3’s Pete Nakos.

The SEC, which is at the forefront of the sudden issue as it houses LSU, released a statement Monday after a videoconference between the presidents and chancellors of the conference, saying “college sports are for college athletes.”

“Individuals who choose to leave college athletics, sign professional playing contracts and compete professionally should not be permitted to then return to college competition,” the statement said.

But why is this even an issue to begin with?

When the NCAA approved a five-for-five eligibility rule, the Class of 2022 was not grandfathered in, meaning their eligibility has run its course. Many players from that group felt slighted, taking legal action in order to earn another year of eligibility.

A U.S. District Court judge in Colorado granted a preliminary injunction, making every athlete from the 2022 class eligible for another year of college.

Matt Campbell was asked last Thursday if he was looking to add anybody from the 2022 class that was deemed eligible, but it was a very quick “no” from Penn State’s head coach.

“We got enough challenges as it is,” Campbell said. “We're just trying to create the best team we can right now internally, and really grateful for the guys that we got with us.”

Then, last Friday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit granted a stay request, essentially pausing that preliminary injunction and once again making those athletes ineligible.

There have been a number of state-court lawsuits, however, that have resulted in eligibility for small groups of players, which is how Wright and a few other players are eligible.

Regardless, the Big Ten’s decision sets a precedent for fellow Power Four conferences regarding the allowance of former professional players back in college football, and other conferences will seemingly follow suit soon. The SEC’s ruling also means Wright cannot return and play for LSU.

Purdy’s scoring was spread out throughout the season, yet it was on full display against Delaware, where she scored two of Penn State’s three goals in a narrow 3-2 win.

title: ‘I’m getting my feel back’ | Max Granville prepares for Penn State return after missing 2025 season
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
It’s been nearly 600 days since Max Granville has seen the field for Penn State.

In less than two weeks, that should change, and he is expected to be a key contributor to the Nittany Lions’ defensive line while hopefully playing his first full season in his collegiate career.

“(I’m) getting my feel back for the game,” Granville said on Tuesday. “I’m getting a feel for things, I feel good.”

Granville showed flashes of success during his freshman season, coming to Happy Valley as the No. 25 edge rusher in his class, per 247sports composite. While he only played in seven games with one tackle in 2024, many were excited about his return for Year 2.

During the offseason, he added weight and improved his run game as he prepared for an increased role. On June 5, 2025, Lions247 first reported Granville sustained a season-ending injury, which was later confirmed by James Franklin to have occurred while he was away from campus during break.

After sitting on the sideline for his entire second year, Granville announced his return for 2026. With a new coaching staff and many new faces along the defensive line, he’s learned the new defensive scheme and rehabbed his injury throughout the spring and summer months.

“(I’m) getting to know the scheme a little more,” Granville said. “I feel like I’ve grown really comfortable with what we’re trying to do on defense.”

Despite being one of the longer-tenured edge rushers on Penn State’s roster, he’s faced a major learning curve. After missing an extended period of time, Granville said practice can sometimes feel like “shooting hands,” but he’s been quick to move past that and get back in the swing of things.

“Really, when I start making plays, I’m like ‘Okay, I’m getting a feel for things,’” Granville said.

During fall camp, Granville’s return has drawn praise from the coaching staff, most of whom are new to his play.

“I think Max Granville would be up (there),” Campbell said. “Man, what he did from the start of practice to where he is today, he’s been remarkable.”

Granville is just one of a few players to have experience playing in front of a full crowd in Beaver Stadium, but has spent the offseason growing with the rest of the defensive ends.

“(The chemistry) is really, really strong,” Granville said. “I feel like we’re a really tight unit.”

As Granville prepares to take the field after missing the 2025 season, he’s embraced the opportunity to be back and support his team.

“Honestly, it’s filled with joy, filled with gratitude,” Granville said. “I can help this team win football games, so it feels really good.”

title: Penn State notebook | DC D’Anton Lynn talks defensive depth, system
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is under two weeks away from beginning the Matt Campbell era, but it also will begin a new era on the defensive side of the ball under D’Anton Lynn.

Lynn’s defensive scheme is continuing to get installed, as some players deal with upwards of their fourth defensive coordinator in as many years.

Lynn met with the media Tuesday to discuss the depth of the defense, the understanding of his system and where he could be working from during games.

Here’s what he had to say.

Defensive depth being put to use

The depth of each position has become no secret, as many players have discussed the benefits of having multiple players who can be reliable. However, it’ll be most shown on the defensive line during the season, given the wear and tear that comes from battling in the trenches.

“We play four to five tackles, and we're probably going to play five guys on the edge,” Lynn said. “Just, it's a long year. You want to keep guys fresh, and then depending on what we're doing that week out of a third down, any of those guys could be on the field.”

The healthy rotation of players has become common in college football, especially in the transfer portal era where the more competitive teams can consistently rotate at a position as important as the defensive line.

Penn State added depth at both the interior and the edge to benefit from a rotation and consistent competitions. With rolling out up to five different players in both spots, it’s an overall attempt to stay as healthy as possible late into the constantly extending college football season.

“With some of the injuries, it's been the next man up, and it's really made guys have to be versatile,” Lynn said. “So there's been some young guys that have stepped up playing different positions. There have been some guys that have started off at this position and now they're doing two because they've had to. But at the end of the day, I feel like it's given us more depth.”

Players understanding his system

Lynn emphasized his players having confidence, and that confidence is growing from understanding his defense that’s still getting installed.

It’s become noticeably apparent to Lynn when a player can step in front of his teammates to explain something.

“I would say like in meeting rooms, just when guys start talking more confidently,” Lynn said. “Like a lot of times, if a guy can get up on the board and he can draw it and he can explain it, you know, he understands it.”

With not a lot of time to fully install his scheme and playbook, Lynn has ensured that he and the players are putting in the work to be ready for Week 1 against Marshall.

“We do a lot of installs as a group,” Lynn said. “We walk through a lot. We watch a lot of tape. We try to hit a bunch of different angles because we never know how guys are.”

In the booth or on the sidelines?

A heavily discussed topic recently has been whether Lynn will be on the sidelines with the players or in the booth. It’s already been confirmed that offensive coordinator Taylor Mouser will be in the booth calling plays on Saturdays, but Lynn’s decision is still up in the air.

Lynn laid out pros and cons to being at each spot and has even tested out both during Penn State’s two scrimmages on the last two Saturdays.

“That was actually my first time calling plays in the booth,” Lynn said. “Pros to the booth, it's the best view. Everything's slower up there. You're away from the emotions of the game.”

Lynn got his first hand look at noticing that everything is slower up top in the booth, but also understands some benefits on the sideline, which he’s done throughout his coaching career.

“The pros to the field are sometimes being with the emotions of the game, I think are a good thing” Lynn said. “So I haven't decided yet, but I did do both.”

Lynn said he’ll likely make the decision by the end of the week to be fully prepared to coach from the spot he decides in the upcoming week.
